title: Gyuto
body: Japanese analog of the western chef's knife — an all-purpose knife. Main difference from a western chef's knife is its thinner blade. As with most Japanese kitchen knives, Gyutos feature much harder steel. Gyutos generally come with a double-grind edge and are made with both western and Japanese (Wa-Gyuto) style handles. The name is sometimes translated as 'Cow Blade.' Exact origins are unclear, but some believe the Gyuto was originally designed for cutting large slices of beef.

title: Wa-Gyuto
body: A Gyuto fitted with a traditional Japanese (Wa) handle. Functionally identical to the standard Gyuto, offering the same all-purpose cutting performance but with the balance, feel, and customizability of a Wa handle.

title: Santoku
body: Full name: Santoku-Bocho. Also called Bunkabocho. In Japanese means 'Knife of Three Virtues,' referring to its versatility with meat, fish, and vegetables. Usually has a short blade up to 200mm, a rounded tip with a slight point, and a double-grind edge. Comes with western or Japanese handles. More versatile than a Nakiri for the home kitchen. The spelling 'Santuko' is an incorrect westernized variant.

title: Bunka Bano-Bocho
body: General purpose knife for cutting fish, meat, and vegetables. 150-170mm blade, Edo-style tip. Not a common term — used primarily by Takeda.

title: Petty
body: Also Petit or Petti naifu. The Japanese equivalent of a paring knife. Blade up to 150mm. The heel is more prominent compared to traditional western paring knives, and it can be used on a cutting board rather than just in-hand.

title: Kiritsuke
body: Also Kiritsuke Hocho. Large, multipurpose kitchen knife. Point is diamond-shaped, like on a Mukimono or Hishigata Usuba. Traditionally a single-grind (chisel) knife. Some makers produce double-grind knives that look like a Kiritsuke, but those are technically a Kiritsuke-geometry Gyuto. A true Kiritsuke is always single-grind. Considered a status symbol among professional chefs in Japan.

title: Funayuki
body: Thinner than a Miroshi Deba but with a wider blade. Standard definition: a knife made specifically for fishermen for ease of handling on boats. Some makers use the same term for thin, double-grind knives with a more Gyuto-like style. Essentially an all-rounder suited for fish, meat, and vegetables.

title: Hakata Bocho
body: Also called Inasa Bocho. A regional variation of the Bunka Bocho from the Hakata area on the southern island of Kyushu. Features a triangular nose and curved spine. Once a staple in any good home kitchen in that region.

title: Satsuma Bocho
body: A regional variation of the Bunka Bocho (home kitchen knife) from the southern Satsuma region on Kyushu island. Has a slightly thicker blade for handling meats and vegetables, and a slightly smaller blade height than a Santoku.

title: Tosagata Bocho
body: A regional variation of the Bunka Bocho (home cooking knife) from the Tosa region of Shikoku island. Light and thin, with a smaller blade height than a Santoku.

title: Makiri
body: Small fishing and utility knife. A simple, versatile knife originally used by fishermen.

title: Reitou Hocho
body: Literally 'freeze knife.' Designated knife for cutting frozen meat. Comes in various shapes and lengths. Short versions are usually serrated; long ones have protrusions on the top to aid cutting and prevent slippage. Two-handled versions are also common.

title: Deba
body: Heavy, thick knife designed for cutting and filleting fish. Can be used for butchering poultry, but cutting bones with it is not recommended. Usually 165-200mm long. Traditionally single-grind. Double-grind versions are called Ryodeba and are quite popular. Mainly used with Japanese-style handles, though western-handled versions (Yo-Deba) exist.

title: Hon-Deba
body: 'Hon' means true or original in Japanese. The Hon-Deba is the thickest and heaviest type of Deba, intended for the most demanding fish-breaking tasks.

title: Atsu Deba
body: 'Atsu' means thick or heavy in Japanese. A generic term for heavy, rough-use Debas. Usually finished in Kuro-uchi (as-forged) style.

title: Ko-Deba
body: A small Deba designed for smaller fish such as sea bream and horse mackerel (Aji).

title: Ai-Deba
body: A slightly lighter Deba with a spine thickness similar to a Miroshi Deba (maybe slightly thinner), and a blade height intermediate between a Miroshi Deba and a Hon Deba.

title: Miroshi Deba
body: Also Mioroshi Deba (more correct spelling). 'Miroshi' means filleting in Japanese. A more slender and longer Deba optimized for the filleting task rather than heavy breaking. The western world commonly uses the slightly incorrect spelling 'Miroshi.'

title: Kako Deba
body: Also Usudeba or Kakou Deba. A knife with a Deba profile but a thinner spine. Used for all-day work by fishmongers.

title: Ryodeba
body: A standard Deba with a double-grind edge. Typically 165-200mm long. Used to fillet fish, dress poultry, and cut through small bones and joints.

title: Yo-Deba
body: Western-style Deba. Typically a double-grind Deba with a western-style handle.

title: Saikachi Deba
body: A specialized Deba with a flat, unpointed tip. Mainly used by fishmongers. Besides general fish-breaking, the unpointed tip is specifically designed to help cut out caviar from the fish. Single-grind; a double-grind version also exists.

title: Kanisaki Deba
body: Specialized Deba for filleting crab, lobster, and shellfish. Unusual design: single-grind, but the edge is ground on the left side for right-handed knives. This prevents the edge from cutting into the crab meat when extracting it from the hard shell. Heavy, thick blade for cutting through the shell.

title: Magurokiri
body: Tuna filleting knife. Extremely long — up to 1000mm — more like a sword than a knife. Used to fillet whole tuna.

title: Oroshi Hocho
body: An extremely long knife, around 1500mm (60 inches) long. Used to cut large tuna in one single stroke. As usual requires more than one person to handle it. Essentially a longer version of the Magurokiri.

title: Sakekiri
body: Also Sake Deba. Salmon knife ('Sake' means salmon in Japanese). Thin, wide knife designed for salmon preparation.

title: Unagisaki
body: 'Unagi' means eel in Japanese; 'saki' means tearing. A small knife for filleting eel. Numerous regional variations exist: Kanto style (Edosaki), Kyoto style, Osaka style, Nagoya style, and Kyushu style. The generic name for all variations is Unagisaki.

title: Dojosaki Bocho
body: Also Anagosaki. Special knife designed for filleting Anago (sea eel) and Dojo (loach, a small eel-related fish caught in local waters in summer). Essentially a thinner and smaller, about 120mm version of the Edosaki knife.

title: Hamokiri
body: Also Honekiri. A heavy knife for slicing pike conger fillet. Hamo (pike conger) has many small bones, so removal is not an option. Instead, incisions are made every 1.25mm or less to cut the bones into small pieces, softening up the flesh. The process itself is called Hamo No Honekiri.

title: Fugubiki
body: Also Fuguhiki. Essentially a thinner version of the Yanagi, slightly flexible for making extremely thin slices of delicate fugu (blowfish) flesh. Fugu is a blowfish in Japanese and is the prestigious sushi ingredient that requires a licensed chef to prepare.

title: Sabasaki
body: A knife for cleaning and filleting saba (mackerel).

title: Tarasaki
body: 'Tara' means cod in Japanese. A specialized knife for breaking down cod. Features a unique indentation in the choil allowing for a greater choke-up grip.

title: Dakketsu
body: A short fisherman's knife used for bleeding tuna or other fish on a boat to keep them fresh after catch.

title: Kujira Hocho
body: 'Kujira' means whale. Originally designed to cut meat and blubber from whales, particularly in the Tosa or Shizuoka regions. Today also used on large fish such as tuna, shark, and swordfish. Very large knives with long handles and blade lengths well over 300mm — the example made by Shinichi Watanabe had a 360mm blade and 25cm handle.

title: Katsuo Hocho
body: Thick, angular-tipped knife for cutting Katsuo (skipjack tuna) and similar fish. Double-grind knife. The angled cutting edge on the front is for sliding down the back to remove tough dorsal fins. Thick enough to handle bones too. Variations include the Umi Bocho (same design but with a more rounded tip).

title: Ikasaki
body: Specialized small knife for breaking down squid. Similar to Makiri but with a more rounded spine and the heel slightly sticking out below the handle.

title: Yanagiba
body: Also Shobu. A long, narrow, single-grind knife, typically well over 240mm. Professional versions of 330mm or even 360mm are fairly common. Designed for cutting raw fish for sashimi and sushi. Usually fitted with a traditional Japanese handle. 'Yanagi' means willow in Japanese, so Yanagiba becomes 'willow leaf blade.' In Western Japan the knife is called Shobu ('iris leaf'). In Tokyo (Eastern Japan) the name Yanagiba is used.

title: Takohiki
body: Also Takobiki. Similar to Yanagi except the tip is square. Designed specifically to cut octopus (Tako in Japanese). Two further variations: Sakimaru Takohiki (round tip) and Kiritsukegata Takohiki (sword tip).

title: Sujihiki
body: Also Sujibiki. Long, narrow, thin blade knife for slicing cooked and raw meats and cleaning fat. 'Suji' means tendon, 'Biki' means pull. The double-grind version of the Yanagiba, commonly used in Western kitchens.

title: Kensaki Yanagiba
body: A Yanagiba with a sword tip (Kensaki), combining the pulling cut of the Yanagi with a more pointed nose.

title: Sushikiri
body: Means 'sushi slicer' in Japanese. Long, approximately 240mm blade, with a symmetrically curved edge. Designed to slice sushi rolls and Hako Sushi (Battera Sushi). Popular in the Kansai area around Osaka and Kyoto. In Tokyo, Yanagi knives are used for the same job.

title: Nakiri
body: Also Nakkiri. Rectangular, thin-bladed vegetable knife. Double-grind. Excels in delicate vegetable cutting. Comes with both western and Japanese handles. The Kakugata (square) style is the most common, also referred to as Kansaigata. The Higashigata (eastern style) variation has a rounded heel and is taller towards the front.

title: Usuba
body: Precisely: Azumagata Usuba (also Kakugata Usuba). A rectangular, thin-bladed vegetable knife similar to the Nakiri but thicker, single-grind, higher quality, and more expensive. Single-grind enables the ultra-precise Katsuramuki (rotary peeling) and Kazarigiri (decorative cutting) techniques. Three types exist: Azumagata (square), Hishigata (diamond, Kanto style), and Kamagata (sickle tip, Kansai style).

title: Kamagata Usuba
body: A Usuba variation with the Kansai-style Kamagata (sickle-shaped) blade tip. Preferred in the Kansai region for vegetable work.

title: Moroha Usuba
body: A double-bevel Usuba. Essentially a Wa-handled Nakiri with a machi and a slightly more acutely angled heel. Not as thick as a normal Usuba. Sizes up to 210mm. Made by Sakai Takayuki and Shigefusa, among others.

title: Mukimono
body: Basically a paring knife with blade geometry similar to a Hishigata Usuba, but thinner and smaller. Mainly used for decorative food carving. Also called Kenmuki.

title: Kawamuki
body: Literally 'skin peeling' knife. Small knife with approximately 90mm long blade, used for peeling and garnishing. Blade geometry is similar to the Kamagata Usuba.

title: Kurimuki
body: In Japanese: chestnut skin peeling knife. Despite its name, works well for peeling, carving, and cutting all kinds of fancy shapes from fruits and small vegetables. Two main variations: Kengata Kurimuki and Kamagata Kurimuki.

title: Muki
body: 'Muki' or 'Muku' means peeling in Japanese. A small, Kamagata-type blade designed for peeling, especially well suited for small items.

title: Honesuki
body: Poultry boning knife. Smaller version of the Garasuki. Features a stiff, triangular blade for breaking down whole birds — particularly chickens. The reverse tanto-style tip allows for precise cuts in tight spaces around joints.

title: Garasuki
body: Poultry boning knife. Bigger version of the Honesuki. Designed in Japanese specialist chicken restaurants for breaking down whole birds. The larger, heavier blade handles bigger poultry.

title: Hankotsu
body: Also called Hankotsu-Maru, Honesuki-Maru, or Sabaki-Nishigata. Japanese-style boning knife. Used to separate bones from meat by cutting with a reverse grip on hanging carcasses. Has a more rounded shape than the angular Honesuki. Also called the 'rebellious knife.'

title: Sabaki
body: 'Sabaki' means butchery or meat breakdown. Can refer to a Honesuki, but there is also a distinct Sabaki shape with a single-grind edge used for butchery work.

title: Kashiwa Deba
body: A special Deba with a flat blade profile, supposedly efficient for skinning fowl.

title: Sobakiri / Udonkiri
body: Also Menkiri (general term for noodle cutting knives). Long, rectangular knife used to cut soba (buckwheat) or udon noodles into thin strips. The blade geometry is blade-heavy with no belly curve, allowing for a clean, straight cut through dough. Sobakiri is specifically for soba; Udonkiri for udon — the knives are essentially the same type.

title: Menkiri
body: The general Japanese name for the category of knives designed for noodle cutting. Includes Sobakiri and Udonkiri. Some makers (e.g. Takeda) use the term for a smaller, cheaper version with blade geometry more resembling a Nakiri — lighter and shorter, but less efficient for cutting noodles.

title: Sasakiri Bocho
body: Extremely specialized knife for cutting bamboo grass/leaves into decorative shapes for presentation with sushi or other expensive foods. 'Sasakiri' is the technique of cutting bamboo grass decoratively.

title: Mochikiri
body: Dedicated knife for cutting Mochi — Japanese rice cake.

title: Chukabocho
body: Japanese term for Chinese Cleaver. A larger, rectangular-shaped, thin-bladed knife for vegetable cutting and general kitchen use.

title: Suikakiri
body: Watermelon knife. Long, thin, rectangular-shaped knife. Blade geometry very similar to the Nakiri.

title: Gishiki Bocho
body: Also Shiki-Bocho. A special knife for imperial court or Shinto Shrine ceremonies. Designed to fillet fish without touching the fish with hands — using only the knife and silver chopsticks. The process is called Shiki-Bocho and requires an extremely skilled chef. The tradition has been practiced in Japan for between 600 and 1000 years.

title: Kaimuki
body: 'Kai' means shellfish and 'muki' means to shuck in Japanese. A small knife designed to open shellfish, scallops, and oysters. Several variations exist.

title: Kaisaki
body: Shellfish paring knife. Also called Hiraki Bocho or Baran-kiri. 'Hiraki' refers to the technique of filleting fish and butterflying them.

title: Kotori Bocho
body: Specialized knife for cutting out fish roe (fully ripe internal ovaries or egg masses of fish and other marine animals, e.g. shrimp, scallop, sea urchins). Usually cod roe. Two blade variations: Kamagata (sickle tip) and Sankakugata (triangular blade).

title: Negikiri
body: Dedicated long onion cutting knife. Two regional styles: Higashigata (Kanto/Eastern style) and Nishigata (Kansai/Western style).

title: Tsuke Bocho
body: Steamed fishcake knife. Used for forming non-solidified fish paste into the correct shape on wooden boards before steaming.

title: Meuchi
body: Not quite a knife but qualifies as one — looks like a railroad spike. An assistant tool when filleting eel with an Unagisaki. The cook drives it through the head of the eel to pin it to the board, then proceeds with the Unagisaki for actual filleting. Comes in plain stiletto and T shapes.

title: Ago
body: Japanese term for the knife chin — the corner spot of the blade heel (Hamato). It is the transition point between the cutting edge and the heel of the blade.

title: Emoto
body: Japanese for 'neck.' Refers to the narrow section of the blade between the blade heel and the handle (or Machi if present). Visible on traditional Japanese knives.

title: Hamato
body: Japanese term for the knife heel — the last few centimeters of the cutting edge closest to the handle. Important for rocking cuts and the finishing pull of a slice.

title: Hawatari
body: Japanese term for blade length — the measurement from the tip to the heel of the blade. On knives with a Machi, different makers measure this differently — some include the Machi, some don't.

title: Kiriba
body: Literally 'blade path.' Refers to the inclined surface that starts at the Shinogi (ridge line), including the cutting edge itself. Essentially the bevel of the blade.

title: Kissaki
body: Japanese term for the blade tip. On single-bevel knives the Kissaki geometry varies by knife type: the Yanagiba has a pointed tip, the Takohiki a square tip.

title: Machi
body: A narrow section of metal approximately 5mm long between the blade neck (Emoto) and the handle, notched to mark the transition. Found on many Japanese knives, never on western knives. Blade length measurements may or may not include the Machi depending on the maker — worth asking if precision matters.

title: Mine / Mune
body: Both Mine and Mune are Japanese terms for the blade spine — the thick, unsharpened top of the blade opposite the cutting edge. Spine thickness is a key factor in the blade's rigidity and cutting feel.

title: Nakago
body: Japanese term for the blade tang — the portion of metal that extends into the handle. Full tang, hidden tang, and rat-tail tang designs all exist in Japanese knives.

title: Shinogi
body: Japanese term for the ridge line formed where the flat portion of the blade meets the blade path (Kiriba). On single-bevel knives the Shinogi is very prominent and is used as a reference when sharpening.

title: Koba
body: Japanese term for the secondary bevel — the small additional bevel at the very edge of the blade, ground at a slightly steeper angle to reinforce the apex. Some high-end Japanese knives are finished without one for maximum sharpness.

title: Kakumaki / Katsura / Kazura
body: Japanese terms for the ferrule or bolster collar — the collar between the blade and the handle that reinforces the junction. Traditionally made from water buffalo horn. Kakumaki is the formal term; Katsura and Kazura are the more commonly used equivalents.

title: Awase
body: Generic Japanese term for clad (laminated) knives. A softer outer layer (Jigane) is clad over a hard steel core (Hagane). There are three types: San-Mai (cladding on both flat sides), Warikomi (cladding on sides and spine), and Ni-Mai (cladding on the edge side only, for single-bevel knives).

title: Hagane
body: The inner layer of hard steel that forms the cutting edge of the blade. Supported and protected by the outer soft layer (Jigane) in laminated Japanese knives. Hagane is typically high-carbon steel — it takes and holds a fine edge but needs the Jigane for resilience.

title: Jigane
body: The soft outer layer of steel that supports and protects the inner hard core (Hagane) in laminated Japanese knives. The quality and finish of the Jigane is important aesthetically — it is the surface that develops the Kasumi finish.

title: San-Mai
body: Cladding technique that laminates a hard steel core (Hagane) with softer outer layers on both flat sides, but not over the spine. The most common lamination style in Japanese kitchen knives. Provides a hard, sharp edge with a tough, forgiving outer structure. Occasionally confused with Warikomi but the two differ in how the cladding wraps the spine.

title: Warikomi
body: Cladding type where the Jigane (soft steel) is applied on the sides AND spine of the Hagane (hard core), encasing it more completely than San-Mai. Occasionally used interchangeably with San-Mai but technically distinct — see cladding diagrams for the difference.

title: Ni-Mai
body: Lamination style used for single-bevel knives. Cladding (Jigane) is applied only on the cutting edge side (Omote); the back (Ura) is left as Hagane — hard steel. The result is visible as the Kasumi finish: hazy soft steel contrasting with the hard, polished edge steel.

title: Honyaki
body: Translates as 'true-forged.' Unlike laminated (Awase) knives, Honyaki knives are made from a single piece of very hard, high-carbon steel throughout. Higher hardness and edge retention than San-Mai knives, but more difficult to forge (hence the high price), more challenging to sharpen, and more prone to chipping or cracking if misused.

title: Mizu-Honyaki
body: Differentially hardened Honyaki knives. The blade spine is coated in clay before quenching in water, making the spine softer and springy while the edge remains extremely hard. The process creates a visible wavy line (Hamon) at the boundary. Considered the pinnacle of Japanese knife construction.

title: Kitaeji
body: Multi-layer Jigane — Damascus-style cladding with a patterned, layered outer steel. The term is often used alongside 'damascus' in the Western market. The pattern appears on the flat sides of the blade and is purely aesthetic on the soft cladding layer; the cutting edge is still a single-steel Hagane core.

title: Kasumi
body: 'Kasumi' means mist in Japanese. Refers to the hazy, matte appearance of the soft Jigane layer next to the hard, polished Hagane on single-bevel (Ni-Mai) knives. The visual contrast between soft and hard steel is part of the traditional aesthetic of Japanese blades.

title: Hon-Kasumi
body: The highest grade of Kasumi finish. Found on premium single-bevel knives where the flatness and contrast of the Kasumi surface are refined to a higher standard. See also Aritsugu Hon-Kasumi Yanagi as a reference example.

title: Kuro-Uchi
body: A rustic as-forged finish — the blade is left with its blackish oxide scale intact except at the cutting edge. Common on working-class Japanese knives by makers like Watanabe and Takeda. Durable, visually striking, and functional: the rough surface reduces sticking.

title: Ishime
body: Roughly translates as 'rock surface.' Similar to Kuro-Uchi but rougher and with more texture — almost like hammered or pebbled stone. Very rare on kitchen knives. Associated with Moritaka.

title: Suminagashi
body: Japanese term for the flowing Damascus pattern on laminated blades. The word itself refers to traditional Japanese ink-marbling art. In knives, the swirling pattern is created by folding and forging the Jigane (cladding) layers.

title: Mokume
body: Japanese term for a wood-grain pattern in steel — can appear in the Jigane (blade cladding), bolster, butt cap, or other fittings. Achieved through special forging techniques that produce a flowing, organic grain pattern resembling wood.

title: Hamon
body: The visible wavy or irregular line on Mizu-Honyaki knives that marks the boundary between the hard edge steel and the softer spine steel. Formed by differential hardening (clay-coating the spine before quenching). A sign of the most demanding traditional forging technique.

title: Ba / Ha
body: Japanese term for knife blade. 'Ba' or 'Ha' is the blade element in compound words like Yanagiba (willow-leaf blade) or Kiriba (blade path). The same character appears in many knife-related compound words.

title: Bocho / Hocho
body: Both Bocho and Hocho mean 'kitchen knife' in Japanese. Neither is used alone — they are always preceded by the knife type (e.g., Nakiri-Bocho, Usuba-Hocho). The pronunciation shifts depending on the compound word.

title: Kiri
body: 'Cutter' in Japanese, derived from the verb 'to cut.' Appears as a suffix in many knife names: Nakiri (cutting greens), Udonkiri (udon cutter), Magurokiri (tuna cutter). One of the most common building blocks in Japanese knife nomenclature.

title: Kirenaga
body: Japanese term for edge retention — how long a knife stays sharp under normal use. A knife with high Kirenaga holds its edge for longer between sharpenings. It is affected by steel hardness, edge geometry, and heat treatment quality.

title: Kaeri
body: Japanese term for the burr — the thin metal wire or fold that forms on the opposite side of the blade during sharpening. Feeling for and properly removing the Kaeri is central to Japanese sharpening technique.

title: Saya
body: A wooden sheath or scabbard for a knife. Traditional Japanese kitchen knives often come with a Saya for storage and travel. The Saya and handle are typically made from the same wood for a matched set.

title: E
body: The Japanese term for the knife handle. Used as the suffix in terms like Wa-E (Japanese handle) or Yo-E (western handle). A fundamental part of the knife's balance and ergonomics.

title: Hirazukuri
body: Sashimi slicing technique where the knife is held perpendicular to the fish and pulled straight back at approximately 45 degrees. Produces clean, flat slices. One of the standard cuts for sashimi preparation.

title: Sogizukuri
body: Sashimi slicing technique where the knife is held at around 40 degrees from the fish surface and pulled back in a slicing motion. Produces wider, thinner slices than Hirazukuri. Good for fish with delicate texture.

title: Usuizukuri
body: Sashimi slicing technique identical to Sogizukuri but producing extremely thin, almost translucent slices of approximately 1mm. Used for very firm fish like flounder. Requires a long, thin knife like a Yanagiba and considerable skill.

title: Yaeizukuri
body: Sashimi slicing technique similar to Hirazukuri, used on tougher-skinned or textured fish. 'Yae' refers to something multilayered. The slices are narrower than standard Hirazukuri cuts.

title: Naruto-giri
body: Literally 'Spiral Tide Cut.' Usually done with a Yanagiba. The knife is held perpendicular to the board. Primarily used for squid: parallel cuts are made on a square piece, which is then turned 90 degrees and rolled. Shiso leaves can be inserted in the spiral.

title: Matsukasa-giri
body: Literally 'Pine Cone Cut.' Usually done with a Yanagiba. The fish slice is cut at an angle to create a lattice or crosshatch pattern. Primarily decorative and used in traditional Japanese cuisine presentation.

title: Kanoko-giri
body: Similar to Matsukasa-giri. Usually done with a Yanagiba with cuts made perpendicular to the board. Used for decorative scoring of fish or other proteins.

title: Utsu
body: The primary cutting technique used with Usuba and Nakiri knives. A combination of push-cutting, vertically downward motion with a slight forward stroke. Different from the rocking-chop technique used with western chef's knives — the flat-bottomed Japanese blade is designed for this straight, vertical-to-forward cut.

title: Honba-Tsuke
body: The process of grinding the real edge onto a knife that was shipped from the manufacturer without one. Some high-end makers (e.g., Aritsugu) ship knives unsharpened and expect the buyer to have this done by a professional sharpener. See also Ura-Oshi.

title: Ura-Oshi
body: Japanese term for flattening the back (Ura) of a single-bevel knife — specifically the concave Urasuki surface. Necessary when the Urasuki has been reduced over many sharpenings. Typically done on a very flat stone before edge sharpening.

title: Omote / Ura
body: The two sides of a single-bevel Japanese knife. Omote is the face side (the bevel side, where the edge is ground). Ura is the back side, which is typically concave (the Urasuki). Understanding which side is which is essential for correct sharpening technique.

title: Urasuki
body: The concave hollow ground on the back (Ura) side of single-bevel Japanese knives. Serves two purposes: reduces drag while cutting (less surface contact), and makes sharpening the flat back easier since only the outer rim needs to contact the stone. Over time, repeated sharpening reduces the Urasuki — requiring Ura-Oshi (re-flattening) to restore it.

title: Hamo No Honekiri
body: The specialized slicing technique used to prepare Hamo (pike conger), a fish with many small, fine bones that cannot be removed. Incisions are made every 1.25mm or less across the fillet to cut the bones into tiny pieces that soften in cooking. Performed with a dedicated Hamokiri knife. Considered one of the most demanding knife skills in Japanese cuisine.

title: Katsuramuki
body: The rotary peeling technique used with a single-bevel Usuba knife to produce a continuous, paper-thin sheet of vegetable (usually daikon or cucumber). Considered the definitive test of Usuba knife skill. Requires extreme precision and can only be done properly with a single-bevel knife.

title: Shiki-Bocho
body: An imperial court or Shinto shrine ceremony in which fish is filleted without the chef ever touching it with their hands, using only a special Gishiki-Bocho knife and silver chopsticks. A tradition practiced in Japan for between 600 and 1000 years, dating at minimum to the early Muromachi period.

title: CPM — Crucible Particle Metallurgy
body: Crucible's proprietary powder metallurgy process, invented circa 1970. Molten metal is poured through a small nozzle with high-pressure inert gas, atomizing the liquid stream into a spray of small, spherical droplets. These fall through a cooling tower, solidify, are screened, collected into sealed containers, and then consolidated using Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP) at near-forging temperatures. Benefits over conventional ingot steel include refined grain size, improved toughness, better wear resistance, easier grinding, and more consistent heat treatment response. CPM is one of the most widely used powder metallurgy processes in premium knife steels.

title: ESR — Electroslag Remelting
body: Secondary steel refining process invented circa 1930, widely adopted about 30 years later. A consumable electrode is dipped into a pool of molten slag inside a water-cooled mold. Electric current (typically AC) superheats the slag, causing drops of metal to melt from the electrode, travel through the slag, and solidify at the bottom of the mold. The refined ingot builds up slowly from the bottom. The slag pool acts as a filter, removing impurities and inclusions. ESR produces high-quality, consistent steel with a clean, homogeneous microstructure. Widely used as a refining step before or after other processes.

title: MM — Micro-Melt (Carpenter Technology)
body: Carpenter Technology's proprietary powder metallurgy process. Metal is first melted using air induction, then poured into an Electroslag Heated (ESH) tundish where it is further purified using a plasma torch to reduce inclusions. The purified molten metal is then atomized with high-pressure inert gas into spherical droplets, collected under a gas shield, and consolidated via Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP). Carpenter's 2nd-generation MM process produces powder particles of 150µm diameter — smaller than Bohler-Uddeholm's 3rd-generation PM powder (250µm) — which is expected to yield similarly fine or finer carbide sizes (2–4µm or smaller). Advantages include refined grain size, improved toughness, wear resistance, and consistent heat treatment response.

title: PM — Powder Metallurgy
body: Broad manufacturing process used for high-performance tool steels since the 1970s. Metal is melted via air induction, purified in an Electroslag Heated (ESH) tundish using graphite electrodes, then atomized with high-pressure inert gas into spherical powder droplets. Droplets are collected and consolidated using Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP). Bohler-Uddeholm's 3rd-generation PM process produces powder of 250µm with carbide sizes of 2–4µm. PM steels offer refined grain size, improved toughness and wear resistance, better grindability, and more predictable heat treatment vs. conventional ingot steels. The process is continuously evolving — manufacturers compete on powder and grain size reduction.

title: MC — Micro Carbide
body: Term used by Henckels (J.A. Henckels) to describe the steel in some of their high-end knives. Functionally equivalent to PM (Powder Metallurgy) steel — the name refers to the fine, uniformly distributed carbides that result from the powder metallurgy process.

title: SF — Spray Form (Osprey Process)
body: Manufacturing technique developed circa 1970. Similar to PM: molten metal is injected into an atomizing tower with high-pressure gas. However, instead of collecting solidified powder, two oscillating nozzles spray semi-solid droplets onto a rotating metal disc (preform) moving upward inside the tower, building up the steel directly. SF has fewer processing steps than PM and produces better properties than conventional ingot steel, making it a more cost-effective middle ground. Carbide size is approximately 10µm — larger than modern PM steels but smaller than typical ingot steels. Good uniformity of carbide distribution throughout the material.

title: VAR — Vacuum Arc Remelting
body: Secondary melting process used to improve alloy quality through microstructural refinement and further purification. The steel is remelted in a vacuum-controlled environment, allowing precise control over solidification. Produces a cleaner, more uniform ingot with fewer inclusions and a refined grain structure. Due to high cost, VAR is not used for most commercially available alloys — reserved for premium or specialty applications where consistency and purity are critical.

title: VIM — Vacuum Induction Melting
body: Process of melting metal under vacuum using electromagnetic induction. Originally developed for exotic metals and alloys, now increasingly used for high-performance alloys across multiple industries. Metal is melted in a vacuum or inert gas environment to prevent oxidation. Chemical reactions, dissociation, and flotation remove dissolved and chemically bonded impurities. The result is an exceptionally clean, homogeneous alloy. Often used as the first step before ESR or VAR in multi-stage refining of premium knife steels.
